steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a machine learning paper on preventing collapse in online deep clustering without data augmentation, by regularizing hard cluster assignments. Explain offline vs. online deep clustering, the collapse problem and the weaknesses of existing fixes, then our Bayesian approach, followed by a contributions list and a paper outline.

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Deep clustering: offline vs. online
  - deep clustering = encode with deep net to feature space, then cluster there
  - offline: process whole dataset, assign all labels at once; online: label each point/batch as processed
  - offline more accurate (some close to supervised performance, cite): use later points for earlier labels
  - but expensive: alternate encoding whole dataset (or training encoder some epochs) and clustering
  - online: joint encode + cluster, cheaper; more versatile, new data constantly arriving vs fixed datasets (cite)
- Collapse and partition support
  - online harder to train: degenerate solution, most points in few clusters; extreme case all in one
  - e.g. intuitive objective: encoding close to own centroid, far from others (clustering params = K-means centroids, first two moments of Gaussian mixture)
  - trivially minimized: encoder maps everything to one point = one centroid
  - techniques against collapse = partition support
  - existing: mostly require data augmentation (DA) (cite); DA-free ones ad hoc, no rigorous foundation (cite)
  - they measure collapse via soft assignments, regularize them toward uniform
  - we: no DA (DA needs prior knowledge for class-preserving augmentations); argue for hard not soft assignments
- Our approach
  - DA-free partition support regularizing hard assignments
  - problem: optimally assign each point in a batch to most appropriate cluster
  - Bayesian framework, prior across clusters (uniform if equally sized)
  - derive precise objective; equivalent up to small error term to maximizing MI of cluster assignments and data index
  - too slow exactly -> greedy approximation, fully online: "combination assignment"
  - beats existing online DA-free methods on four image clustering datasets; high-quality representations
  - hard vs. soft analysis; converting soft to hard != regularizing hard
  - hard vs. soft studied before (cite), new in context of online deep clustering collapse
- Contributions (4 bullets)
  - Bayesian framework, avoids unrealistic per-batch uniformity assumption
  - objective, proof of approx. equivalence to MI maximization
  - empirical: beats partition support methods, better accuracy, more informative representations
  - further analysis justifying focus on hard assignments
- Organization: Section 2 related work; Section 3 theory, greedy algorithm, MI equivalence proof; Section 4 results and analysis; Section 5 summary

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Deep clustering means combining deep learning and clustering: the data is first encoded with a deep neural network into a feature space, and then the clustering is done in this feature space. Clustering models can be offline or online. Offline models process the whole dataset and then assign all the cluster labels at once. Online models instead assign a cluster label to each data point, or each batch, as it is processed. Offline methods can give more accurate clusterings (e.g., some offline methods get close to supervised performance), since they can use information from later data points when they assign cluster labels to earlier ones. But they are more expensive to train, because they have to alternate between encoding the whole dataset, or training the encoder for some number of epochs, and clustering the encoded data. Online models can encode and cluster jointly, so they are less computationally expensive. They are also more versatile, because they can be used in real-world settings where new data keeps becoming available, while offline methods are limited to fixed pre-defined datasets.

The downside of online methods is that they are harder to train. In particular there is a risk of a degenerate solution, where most of the data points end up in a small number of clusters. In the extreme case, all the points are put into the same cluster. For example, an intuitive way to set up training for online deep clustering is to update both the encoder network and the clustering parameters so that the encoding of each point is close to its cluster centroid and far from the other cluster centroids. (The clustering parameters are e.g., the centroids in K-means or the first two moments in a Gaussian mixture model.) But this objective is trivially minimized if the encoder network maps all data points to the same point in feature space, and this point is equal to one of the cluster centroids. We call techniques for avoiding this collapse partition support. Several partition support methods have been proposed, but most of them need data augmentation (DA), and the ones that don't are often ad hoc and don't have a rigorous technical foundation. Also, they take the soft assignments as the measure of partition collapse, and they regularize the soft assignments to make them more uniform. This paper focuses on deep clustering without DA. This is an advantage, because a method that relies on DA is limited to domains where there is enough prior knowledge to do class-preserving augmentations. We also argue that soft assignments are not an accurate measure of collapse, and that we should focus on hard assignments instead.

- Our approach
  - DA-free partition support, regularize hard assignments
  - assign each point in a batch to most appropriate cluster; Bayesian framework with prior across clusters (uniform if equally sized)
  - precise objective, equivalent up to small error to maximizing MI of cluster assignments and data index
  - greedy approximation -> fully online "combination assignment"
  - beats online DA-free methods on four image clustering datasets; good representations
  - hard vs. soft analysis; converting soft to hard is not regularizing hard; relation studied before, new for online collapse
- Contributions
  - Bayesian framework (no per-batch uniformity assumption)
  - objective + approx. equivalence to MI maximization
  - empirical gains over partition support methods
  - analysis justifying hard assignments
- Organization: Sections 2-5

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Deep clustering means combining deep learning and clustering: the data is first encoded with a deep neural network into a feature space, and then the clustering is done in this feature space. Clustering models can be offline or online. Offline models process the whole dataset and then assign all the cluster labels at once. Online models instead assign a cluster label to each data point, or each batch, as it is processed. Offline methods can give more accurate clusterings (e.g., some offline methods get close to supervised performance), since they can use information from later data points when they assign cluster labels to earlier ones. But they are more expensive to train, because they have to alternate between encoding the whole dataset, or training the encoder for some number of epochs, and clustering the encoded data. Online models can encode and cluster jointly, so they are less computationally expensive. They are also more versatile, because they can be used in real-world settings where new data keeps becoming available, while offline methods are limited to fixed pre-defined datasets.

The downside of online methods is that they are harder to train. In particular there is a risk of a degenerate solution, where most of the data points end up in a small number of clusters. In the extreme case, all the points are put into the same cluster. For example, an intuitive way to set up training for online deep clustering is to update both the encoder network and the clustering parameters so that the encoding of each point is close to its cluster centroid and far from the other cluster centroids. (The clustering parameters are e.g., the centroids in K-means or the first two moments in a Gaussian mixture model.) But this objective is trivially minimized if the encoder network maps all data points to the same point in feature space, and this point is equal to one of the cluster centroids. We call techniques for avoiding this collapse partition support. Several partition support methods have been proposed, but most of them need data augmentation (DA), and the ones that don't are often ad hoc and don't have a rigorous technical foundation. Also, they take the soft assignments as the measure of partition collapse, and they regularize the soft assignments to make them more uniform. This paper focuses on deep clustering without DA. This is an advantage, because a method that relies on DA is limited to domains where there is enough prior knowledge to do class-preserving augmentations. We also argue that soft assignments are not an accurate measure of collapse, and that we should focus on hard assignments instead.

We propose a partition support that does not need DA and that regularizes hard assignments. Specifically, we look at the problem of how to optimally assign each data point in a batch to the most appropriate cluster. We write this problem probabilistically in a Bayesian framework, where the regularizing part is captured by a prior across clusters. If the clusters are equally sized, this prior can be uniform. We then use this expression to derive a precise optimization objective, and we show that it is equivalent, up to a small error term, to maximizing the mutual information of the cluster assignments and the data index. This objective is too slow to solve exactly, but we come up with a greedy approximation algorithm that is straightforward to implement and gives an intuitive method for fully online clustering, which we call combination assignment. The method outperforms existing online DA-free clustering methods on four popular image clustering datasets. We also analyze the underlying representations and show that they are of high quality. Finally, we analyze the role of hard vs. soft cluster assignments in our partition support method and in previous methods, and we argue that regularizing hard assignments is more effective. Existing methods can easily convert soft assignments to hard assignments, but this is very different from regularizing the hard assignments, which is what we propose. The relation between hard and soft clustering has been studied before, but studying it in the context of regularizing online deep clustering collapse is new.

Our main contributions are summarized below.

- We give a clear Bayesian framework for the problem of hard assignments in online deep clustering models, which avoids the unrealistic assumption made by most existing methods that each batch is uniform.
- We use the framework to derive an optimization objective and we prove that it is approximately equivalent to maximizing the mutual information of the cluster assignments and the data index.
- We show empirically that the resulting method is significantly better than existing partition support methods at avoiding partition collapse, it improves clustering accuracy, and it leads to more informative representations.
- We do further analysis of how different partition support methods perform, which justifies our choice to focus on hard assignments.

The rest of the paper is organized like this. Section 2 gives an overview of related work. Section 3 lays out the theoretical foundations of our method, describes the greedy algorithm for optimizing the objective, and proves the equivalence to mutual information maximization. Section 4 reports our empirical results and analysis, and Section 5 summarizes our findings.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Deep clustering refers to the combination of deep learning and clustering, where the data are first encoded with a deep neural network to a feature space, and clustering is then performed in that feature space. Clustering models can be classified as offline or online. Offline models process the entire dataset and then assign all cluster labels at once, whereas online models assign a cluster label to each data point, or each batch, as it is processed. Offline methods can produce more accurate clusterings (e.g., [1,2] reaching close to supervised performance), as they can leverage information from later data points when assigning cluster labels to earlier ones. However, they are more expensive to train, since they must alternate between encoding the entire dataset, or training the encoder for some number of epochs, and clustering the encoded data. Online models, on the other hand, can jointly encode and cluster, and are therefore less computationally expensive. They are also more versatile, being applicable in real-world settings where new data constantly become available, as opposed to offline methods, which are limited to fixed pre-defined datasets [3].

The disadvantage of online methods is that they are more difficult to train. In particular, they risk producing a degenerate solution in which the large majority of data points are concentrated in a small number of clusters; in the extreme case, all points are placed into the same cluster. For example, an intuitive training procedure for online deep clustering is to update both the encoder network and the clustering parameters so that the encoding of each point is close to its cluster centroid and far from other cluster centroids. (The clustering parameters are e.g., the centroids in K-means or the first two moments in a Gaussian mixture model.) However, this objective is trivially minimized by the encoder mapping all data points to the same point in feature space, equal to one of the cluster centroids. We refer to techniques for avoiding collapse as partition support. Several partition support methods have been proposed, but they mostly require data augmentation (DA) [4,5], and those that do not are often ad hoc and lack a rigorous technical foundation [6,7]. Additionally, they take the soft assignments as a measure of partition collapse and regularize the soft assignments to make them more uniform. This paper focuses on deep clustering without DA, which is an advantage, because relying on DA limits a method to domains where sufficient prior knowledge for class-preserving augmentations is available. We further argue that soft assignments are not an accurate measure of collapse, and that we should focus on hard assignments instead.

We propose a DA-free partition support that regularizes hard assignments. Specifically, we consider how to optimally assign each data point in a batch to the most appropriate cluster. We express this problem probabilistically in a Bayesian framework, where the regularizing element is captured by a prior across clusters, which can be uniform in the case of equally-sized clusters. We then use this expression to derive a precise optimization objective, which we show to be equivalent, up to a small error term, to maximizing the mutual information of the cluster assignments and the data index. This objective is too slow to solve exactly, but we devise a greedy approximation algorithm that can be implemented straightforwardly and yields an intuitive method for fully online clustering, which we term combination assignment. This method outperforms existing online DA-free clustering methods on four popular image clustering datasets, and we show that its underlying representations are of high quality. Finally, we analyze the role of hard vs. soft cluster assignments in our partition support method and in previous methods, and make the case that regularizing hard assignments is the more effective approach. Note that, although existing methods can easily convert soft assignments to hard assignments, this is very different from regularizing the hard assignments, as we propose. While the relation between hard and soft clustering has been studied before [8,9], its study in the context of regularizing online deep clustering collapse is new.

Our main contributions are briefly summarized below.

- • We articulate a clear Bayesian framework for the problem of hard assignments in online deep clustering models, which avoids the unrealistic assumption of uniformity in each batch made by most existing methods.

- • We use this framework to derive an optimization objective and prove that it is approximately equivalent to maximizing the mutual information of the cluster assignments and the data index.

- • We show empirically that the resulting method significantly outperforms existing partition support methods in avoiding partition collapse, improving clustering accuracy and leading to more informative representations.

- • We further analyze the performance of different partition support methods, which justifies our choice to focus on hard assignments.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 gives an overview of related work, and Section 3 lays the theoretical foundations of our method, describes our greedy algorithm for optimizing the resulting objective, and proves the equivalence to mutual information maximization. Section 4 reports our empirical results and analysis, and Section 5 summarizes our findings.
